title: Socio-demographic and lifestyle influences on falls among the elderly persons living in Gatanga Sub-county, Murang’a County, Central Kenya: A cross-section study
author: Ernest Kimani

steps_raw.instruction: Socio-demographic and lifestyle influences on falls among the elderly persons living in Gatanga Sub-county, Murang’a County, Central Kenya: A cross-section study
Ernest Kimani1*, Simon Karanja2¶, Lawrence Muthami3¶
1Department of Surgery and Orthopedics, Embu Level V Hospital, Embu County, Kenya
2Department of Public and Community Health, College of Health Sciences, Jomo Kenyatta University of Agriculture and Technology, Kiambu County, Kenya
3Center for Public Health Research, Kenya Medical Research Institute, Nairobi, Kenya

An estimated third of the elderly people worldwide sustain falls every year, which contributes to over 20% of injuries in this age group. In central region of (Mount) Kenya, despite increasing awareness on the condition, the magnitude, socio-demographic and lifestyle factors leading to falls in the elderly are not well known.

The main objective of this study was to investigate the prevalence of falls, their outcomes and the factors influencing their occurrence among the elderly persons living in Gatanga Sub-county, Murang’a County, central region of Kenya. An analytical cross-sectional study design was used. Using systematic random sampling, 420 out of 9146 study participants were identified and interviewed at home. Using a structured interview form, data was collected on socio-demographic, socio-economic, lifestyle and medical factors, and fall or non-fall status from September 2016 to August 2017. Statistical analysis was done with STATA 13.0 to establish the distribution and characteristics of falls.

The prevalence of falls amongst the elderly in this region is high at 42%. The farming lifestyle involving crop farming and animal husbandry, socio-economic factors and medical illnesses are significantly associated with falls. To reduce the occurrence of falls, it requires understanding of the underlying factors leading to falls and integration of relevant preventive measures that reduce the risk of falls in specific communities of the elderly.
Elderly, falls, fractures, injuries, Kenya
Fall – a sudden unintentional coming to rest from a level ground with or without loss of consciousness, excluding fall from height and high energy push by moving objects.
Circumstances of fall – an action or event immediately preceding or directly leading to a fall.
Elderly – a person aged 65 years old and above.

A fall is one of the causes of unintentional injury. In the International Classification of Disease-10 (ICD-10) falls are coded as W00-W19. These codes encompass a wide range of falls including falls on the same level, upper level and other unspecified falls (1). A fall is normally defined as, “inadvertently coming to rest on the ground, floor or other lower level, excluding intentional change in position to rest in furniture, wall or other objects” (2).

It is estimated that approximately one third of elderly people aged 65 years and above, all over the world fall annually (3). Studies across Europe (4, 5) Middle East (6) and Africa (7, 8) show falls rates ranging between 20% to 40%.

In Kenya, falls are known to contribute significantly to injuries among elderly people. A study in Kenyatta National Hospital, the largest referral hospital in Kenya, showed that falls were the second leading cause of trauma and hospitalization among the elderly aged 60 years and above with a frequency of 41.4% after road traffic accidents (44.7%). Among the fallers, 75% were due to falls on the same level (9). Falls were also cited as a leading cause of domestic injuries among the elderly aged 55 years and above seen in health facilities in Nairobi area, Kenya, contributing to 69% of the injuries (10). The incidence of hip fractures, a common outcome of falls is also on the increase in Kenya (11). Over 90% of hip fractures occur as a result of falls (12).

A trauma related mortality study in Western Kenya showed that falls were a leading cause of deaths especially among females. Mostly affected (88%) were elderly persons aged 65 years and above with resulting broken limbs, back, neck or pelvis, hence complications leading to death (13).

Falls occur due to complex interaction of biological, demographic, physical and environmental factors. Biological factors such as old age, female gender (14) and medical conditions (15) have been associated with a higher risk of falling. Data shows that fall-related injuries are approximately 4.0% among 65-69 year olds and 7.0% among persons over 80 years (16, 17). Demographic factors contributing to falls include race where whites are at a higher risk of falling than blacks (18). Unfavorable socio-economic factors such as limited access to health services, illiteracy, poor housing and low income are associated with increased risk of chronic diseases hence falls (19). Physical factors such as visual impairment (20), lower limb arthritis (21), gait variability (22), muscle weakness and lower limb strength (23, 24), foot problems (25, 26), cognitive impairment (27), and low and high body mass index (28, 29) have also been found to increase the risk of falling. Environmental factors that increase the risk of falling include slippery floors, staircases and reduced lighting (30).

Consequences of falls include admission in nursing homes, depression, immobilization, loss of autonomy, abandonment of daily activities, isolation, head injuries, confusion, fear of falling, fractures and death among others (31, 32, 33). The economic and social burden arising from falls is also high (34, 35, 36).

Preventing falls can significantly reduce morbidity and mortality from falls related injuries and complications and improve the quality of life among the elderly. Majority of the falls can be prevented. To prevent falls, it is important to identify the modifiable risk factors and come up with culturally appropriate and effective evidence based methods (2, 3, 37, 38).

Availability of data on incidence, prevalence and risk factors of falls among the elderly in Sub-Saharan Africa region is very limited since there are very few studies existing on the subject (39). In the central (Mount) Kenya region, despite increasing awareness on falls as a significant contributor of morbidity among the elderly people, little is known on their magnitude and the socio-demographic, lifestyle, and medical influence on their occurrence among the elderly of this region. Factors such as terrain of the region which is largely mountainous, increasing prevalence of non-communicable diseases such as diabetes (40), low socio-economic status, the farming lifestyle and inaccessibility to quality healthcare services are hypothesized to lead to a higher incidence of falls in these communities. The vast majority of elderly people in Kenya live in rural areas.

This study set out to accomplish the following specific objectives; 1) To determine the prevalence of falls, their characteristics, associated complications and circumstances of their occurrence among the elderly persons living in Gatanga Sub-county of Central Kenya region 2) To assess the socio-demographic, lifestyle, socio-economic and medical factors of the elderly. 3) To establish the association between falls and socio-demographic, lifestyle, socio-economic and medical factors in the elderly.
A community based cross–sectional study was conducted between 4th – 15th September, 2017 in Gatanga Sub-county of Murang’a County.

Gatanga Sub-county, Murang’a County, is located in the mountainous central region of Kenya (Mount Kenya region). It covers an area of 599 km2 (square kilometers). Majority of the people living in the area are of Kikuyu ethnicity and engage in a farming lifestyle involving crop farming and rearing of domestic animals (41). Reports from Thika Level 5 sub-county hospital and other local hospitals indicate that falls are a significant cause of morbidity among elderly patients from the region, with women mostly affected resulting in hip and long bone fractures, head injuries, bruises and long term effects such as immobilization and loss of independence (42).

A list of households and the elderly persons residing in a location represented by a Community Health Unit (CHU) was retrieved from the existing household health records of a CHU contained with the Community Health Workers (CHW). A total of 6127 potential households were identified.

Using systematic random sampling, households where interviews would be conducted were selected. The first household to be interviewed was selected using simple random sampling from the 1st fifteen households in the area. Interviewers were required to move in one direction systematically starting from the main street of their study area.

On encounter with a selected household, the interviewer, a local CHW, administered the inclusion and exclusion criteria. In case of more than one eligible member, a one shilling coin was tossed with males as head and females as tail to select the member to be interviewed. If an eligible member was not present in a household during the initial visit, the interviewer was required to revisit the household at a later time or date to undertake the interview. If a household did not have an eligible member based on the inclusion and exclusion criteria, the next household with an eligible member on the sampling list was selected.
Inclusion and Exclusion criteria
Those included in the study were,
Elderly persons aged 65 years and above.
Residents of Gatanga Sub-county for the last 1 year.
Those excluded from the study,
Disabled elderly persons with physical disabilities limiting use of both feet for walking and use of arms for support occurring before the preceding one year.

Not able to give information due to severe mental incapacitation. This was assessed prior to undertaking the main interview. An eligible participant was assessed on correct orientation of time, place and person. And on ability to undertake general activities of daily living such as self-feeding, self-bathroom care, self-grooming and maintaining a ‘normal’ interaction and conversation with close contacts and interviewer. Collaborative information (where applicable) on mental history specifically bizarre behavior was briefly sought from persons who were closely associated with the study participant. In other cases, the Community Health Workers used their knowledge of participants based on past interactions with the participants. CHWs are trained volunteers from their respective communities where they participate in delivery of primary health care services.

The main outcome variable for this study was a reported fall in the preceding one year, September 2016 to August 2017. A fall was defined as any sudden unintentional coming to rest from a level ground with or without loss of consciousness, excluding falls from heights, falls involving bicycles, motorcycles and vehicles and falls due to direct aggressive push by farm animals such as cows, donkeys and goats.

Further information collected on falls included, the number of falls events sustained during the reference period of study, time and place of last fall, whether accompanied by someone or not during the fall and the immediate circumstances leading to the fall.

Complications of falls included immobilization, fear of falling, abandonment of daily activities, loss of autonomy, hospitalization and associated injuries such as skin bruises, fractures, head injury and confusion.
Exposure variables were collected on socio-demographic characteristics including age, gender, marital status and the level of education.

Medical information sought included, current use of medications, alcohol and cigarettes smoking. Whether one was on active treatment for illnesses including diabetes, hypertension, heart disease, kidney disease, joints pains (involving the ankle, knees, hip, fingers, wrist, elbow and shoulder), lower back pains, recent or recurrent syncope, cancer, stroke, anemia, depressed mood and acute stress, headache, peripheral neuropathy, wounds and pressure sores, bruises and cuts, recent acute illnesses and altered mental states. Foot problems investigated included foot pains and infestation with jiggers.

Frailty of elderly persons was established using Frailty for Non-Disabled index questionnaire (43) (S1 Appendix 1(B)), unsteadiness in gait/problems with walking or balance and difficulty in doing usual activities.

Nutrition status of the elderly persons was evaluated using a Mini Nutrition Assessment – Short Form (MNA-SF) (S1 Appendix 1(C)). This is a tool that has been used to assess the nutritional status of the elderly persons (44, 45).

A Modified Barthel Index of activities of daily living was used to assess the functional capacity of the elderly persons (S1 Appendix 1(D)). A modified Barthel Index is a tool with a set of indicators used to assess the activities of daily living of disabled persons (46).

Social-economic, lifestyle and environmental factors were investigated and the variables listed under this included the type of floor of the residential house, source of lighting at night, living alone or with someone, involvement in daily activities, attending to domestic animals and source of funds to cater healthcare expenditure.
Data sources / measurement

Data was collected from 4th – 15th September, 2017 where seventeen trained interviewers visited the study participants’ homes to administer the structured interview forms (S1 Appendix 1). The reference period for the study was September 2016 to August 2017.
The interviewers were Community Health Workers of their respective areas. Sources of data included, the study participants, their caretakers, and past health records.
Recall bias. Collaborative history was however sought from the caretakers and existing medical records were used to validate lifestyle, illness history and medications.

Assuming a 50% prevalence rate of falls in the elderly, a sample of 384 elderly persons was calculated for estimating the expected proportion with 5% absolute precision and 95% confidence interval. The sample was inflated to 424 assuming a non-response rate of 10%.
Statistical methods / data analysis
Hard copy data was converted to soft copy data using the Epi Info version 3.5.4. Statistical analysis was done using statistical Software Package STATA 13.0 (StataCorp, College Station, Texas).

Descriptive statistics including mean, mode and median with 95% confidence intervals were computed to estimate age and sex distribution of participants, the distribution of medical conditions, social economic and lifestyle factors associated with the falls and the frequency and characteristics of falls. Proportions were reported as a percentage of the collected data. Data was presented in bar graphs and summary tables.

For significance testing in bivariate analysis, Pearson’s Chi Square Test was used for categorical variables and p<0.05 was considered statistically significant (47). Subsequently, those variables statistically significant (𝑃-value <0.10) in the bivariate analysis were entered into a logistic regression model to evaluate the independent associations between falls and characteristics of the participants. Results of the regression model were presented as odds ratios (OR) with their 95% confidence intervals (95% CI) (48).
Ethical considerations
The research protocol (ref. KEMRI/SERU/CPHR/09/3509) was approved by Scientific and Ethical Review Unit (SERU) of Kenya Medical Research Institute on 21th August, 2017 (49).

Four hundred and twenty-four study participants were interviewed. Analysis was done for 420 participants excluding four. Interviews were erroneously done on two participants who were younger than expected as per the eligibility criteria while the other two were disabled on a wheelchair having sustained the disability prior to reference period for the study. Hence data was analyzed and reported for 420 study participants.

Prevalence, characteristics, outcomes and circumstances of falls

The prevalence rate of falls for the period of study, September 2016 to August 2017 was 42.14% (CI 37.37 - 47.02%). In relation to gender, 45.3% of females and 34.7% of males had sustained a fall during the study period.

The characteristics of falls investigated showed that majority of fallers (66.2%) had recurrent falls. Most falls occurred in the outdoors (79.7%) and during daytime (78.5%), especially in the morning hours. Majority of the fallers (57.1%) reported to have fallen on a flat surface while most of them (67.2%) were accompanied by someone during the last fall episode.

Study participants reported various circumstances leading to their falling (Figure 1). These included walking (37.6%), postural change (11.5%), sliding (7.9%), fell while working (6.7%), tripped by goats while attending to them (5.5%), felt dizzy then fell (5.5%), under influence of alcohol (5.5%), tripped by an object (3.6%), missed a step (3.6%), lost balance, lost perception of a place while in darkness, delirium like states, tremors, loss of energy and ankle twist.

This study investigated the occurrence of falls amongst the elderly in Gatanga region of Kenya in the context their socio-demographic, lifestyle and medical influence. The results show that interaction of these factors is likely to have a significant influence on falls in the elderly. Understanding the root causes of falls in this population will provide potential areas for address when coming up with suitable fall prevention measures.

In this study the prevalence of falls was 42.14% (CI 37.37 - 47.02). This prevalence is relatively high and is consistent with other studies in different places of Africa and the world which have shown the falls prevalence of 20-60% (3, 7, 39, 50). Introduction of robust falls prevention measures would likely reduce the prevalence.

The socio-demographic, cultural and lifestyle factors such as engagement in crop farming and animal husbandry was significantly associated with falls. Interaction between elderly persons and domestic animals was identified as a potential risk factor for falls. Nine study participants reported to have fallen while attending to goats, having been pulled or tripped suddenly by their tethering ropes. Other elderly persons reported to have fallen while carrying fodder in the farms and when going to farms. This shows that the farming lifestyle of elderly persons in this region is a possible contributor to falls. Previous studies have not shown this association between the farming lifestyle and falls. Thus when developing falls prevention strategies, it is important to understand the cultural and lifestyle factors of the elderly and how these factors influence the risk of falls.

Payment of hospital bills by relying on relatives or well-wishers was positively associated with falls. 60.9% of the elderly paid hospital bills using health insurance (7.3%) or their own cash (53.6%) whereas 39.1% paid using relatives or well-wishers’ contributions. This implies that the group which depended on relatives or well-wishers for health care lacked financial independence to support their own hospital visits. This was likely to limit their accessibility to health services which made them likely to fall due to failure to have illnesses which could predispose them to falls treated. High levels of poverty have been found among the elderly persons in this region. Poor socio-economic status leading to inaccessibility to health services has been said to be a risk factor for falls. Some of the possible causes of poor socio-economic status among elderly include lack of income, lack of adequate social protection, neglect and abandonment by their children and a higher burden of diseases (51).

Terrain of a region has been said to influence falls. In this study there were no significant associations that were established between the self-reported terrain of fall and falls occurrence. However, the data was collected from two distinct regions of the Gatanga sub-county, the upper mountainous zone and the lower relatively flat region. The upper mountainous Gatanga zone had a falls prevalence of 50% (N=314), whereas the lower flat Gatanga area had a falls prevalence of 18% (N=106). There were significant differences in the prevalence of falls between the two zones, (χ2 (420) = 31.50, 0.000). Geographical topography of a region is thought to be an important environmental predictor of falls. A study in Equador in 2013 showed an increased fall rate among people living in mountainous zones than relatively flat coastal regions (52).

Other factors which were significantly associated with the falls in this population included, being female, actively engaging in crop farming and depending on relatives/well-wishers for hospital bills payment rather than having own cash or health insurance policy. Medical and lifestyle factors such as current medications use, having lower back pains, memory loss, diabetes, syncope/fainting, blindness, headache, neck pains, hearing impairment, wounds, difficulty in carrying out usual activities, and being frail as measured in the Frailty for non-disabled index tool.

Dizziness and unsteadiness in gait or problems with walking or balance were negatively associated with the falls. These factors possibly limited movement in the elderly persons hence the negative association with falls.

Despite attempts to collect information which represented the true status of health of the elderly persons, there were limitations which could have interfered with the internal validity of the results. Such included challenges with memory and indeed 43.8% of the participants, reported to have memory loss. Hence the cross-section design of the study where we measured exposure and outcome variables at the same time could result in some level of bias where they could have understated the frequency of fall episodes.

However, a study in Brazil tested the agreement between the self-reported method after 12 months versus the prospective method and it was found the global agreement was 79% for falls and 89% for recurrent falls (53). This shows that the self-report method at 12 months has a capacity to provide fairly reliable information on the falls to derive reliable estimates. However, it is required to practice caution when using such method to investigate the epidemiology of falls.
Similarly, the process of establishing the true illness status in some situations due to lack of medications and medical records. However, several methods were used to address this.
The study participants to provide medications they were currently on and hospital records such as prescriptions and visit cards which they had at the time of the interview.
Collaborative information was sourced from close family members and close contacts to ascertain treatment for illnesses as described by the elderly persons.
Almost all (over 95%) of our study participants had either of these information sources, nevertheless there was still a chance of misclassification bias.

Establishment of true mental status among the elderly may have lacked precision owing to lack of a validated tool to use in a largely illiterate population. However, we enquired on orientation to time, place and person among the sampled study participants, their behavior on whether there were any largely abnormal behaviors noted recently, ability to maintain a ‘normal’ interaction and conversation with close contacts and interviewer and the ability to undertake day to day activities such as self-feeding, self-grooming, self-bathroom use, and we also used collaborative history on lifestyle and past medical history of the study participants from their care givers and close contacts.
The cross-section design of our study could not prove the temporal direction of association between some exposure variables and the outcomes. Wounds and syncope would have occurred due to falls.

The life expectancy in Kenya has been increasing due to increasing standards of living thus the population of the elderly persons is also increasing (54). The resulting burden of disease from falls and the related illnesses is likely to be high given that there are no specific public health intervention measures in place to address the problem.

The World Health Organization Falls Prevention Model recognizes the pillars of preventing falls as; (1) awareness building; (2) individual assessment of environmental and societal factors that increase the likelihood of falls; and 3) facilitating the design and implementation of culturally appropriate evidence based interventions that will significantly reduce the number of falls among older persons (3).

Research on falls need to be prioritized to understand the trends of falls among the elderly of this region. This will help in planning and resource mobilization. Research will also promote understanding of the environmental and individual factors that increase the likelihood of falling, and identify appropriate evidence based interventions that are likely to mitigate the situation in specific communities.

There is need to target health workers, the community and elderly persons with relevant falls prevention messages and information on the risk factors and need for health check-ups for the elderly. Recurrent falls are likely to lead to severe injuries and fractures and could signify an underlying problem.

Improved accessibility to healthcare among elderly persons is of high importance. Elderly people have a higher burden of diseases that are likely to make them prone to falling. Access to quality healthcare services should be made easier for them to ensure that they seek early medical intervention to prevent falls, severe injuries and incapacitation.

The socio-demographics and lifestyle of the elderly persons in the central region of Kenya is largely very similar. The region is mountainous, inhabited by people of the Kikuyu ethnicity who majority engage in crop and animal farming lifestyle. An informal survey of elderly persons admitted with fractures in the different hospitals in the region show very similar causes of fall related injuries. Such include mostly females, being tripped by goats, sliding on a wet surface, sustaining falls while walking or carrying farm materials and other etiologies as elaborated in the discussion and shown in Figure 1. Thus the findings of this study are likely to apply to other areas of central (Mount) Kenya region.
